'''Swamp key''' is an item dropped from [[The Elder]] after defeating him. It is used to open [[Sunken Crypts]] in [[Swamp]] [[biomes]].

==Availability==
*Dropped from [[The Elder]] in the [[Black Forest]].

==Usage==
The Swamp Key is used to unlock [[Sunken Crypts]] inside the [[Swamp]]. It must be in the player's inventory the first time each crypt gate is opened, but is no longer needed to re-enter the same crypt. It can be used an unlimited amount of times.

The '''Megingjord''' is a belt that can be purchased from [[Haldor]].

== Usage ==
The belt grants the player superhuman strength, allowing them to carry 150.0 more [[carry weight|weight]] when equipped. This is represented as an effect on the character.

It is equipped in the accessory slot, and thus allows players to wear a full set of armor in addition to the belt. The Megingjord conflicts with the [[Wishbone]] and the [[Wisplight]], which occupies the same equipment slot.

== Notes ==
* The belt is a direct reference to [[wikipedia:Megingjörð|Megingjörð]], the belt of Thor, the Norse god of thunder. In mythos, the belt shares the same capabilities as the one in-game, granting the user superhuman strength.
* When equipped, a message will appear for the player stating "You feel stronger."

The '''Wishbone''' is an accessory gained by killing the boss [[Bonemass]] in the [[Swamp|Swamps]].
== Usage ==
After equipping the Wishbone, the player will gain a buff allowing them to find secrets underground. While equipped, the player will intermittently see a puff of green particles around them and hear a ding, beginning approximately 20 meters from a secret.
[[File:ValheimWishbone.gif|alt=The particle effect the Wishbone makes when it finds a nearby secret.|left|thumb|The wishbone rapidly pulsing directly above a secret.]]
As the player gets closer to the secret, the dinging will get both faster and higher pitch, and the puffs of green particles will occur more frequently. Once above the secret, the player can dig to reveal [[Muddy Scrap Pile]]s ([[Swamp]]), [[Silver Ore|Silver veins]] ([[Mountain]]), or [[Treasure|Buried Treasure]] ([[Meadows]]). 

Once the object is interacted with (opened or mined) the Wishbone will stop detecting that object. 

The Wishbone conflicts with the [[Megingjord]] and the [[Wisplight]], which occupy the same equipment slot.

'''Tankards''' are items used to consume [[:Category:Mead|mead]] from within an inventory. Mead can, however, be consumed without the use of a tankard.

== Notes ==
* The description "Skål!" is Swedish, Norwegian and Danish for "toast!", or "cheers!"
* The [[Horn of Celebration]] is a special tankard marking the one-year anniversary of the release of ''[[Valheim]]''.
* The [[Dvergr Tankard]] is a rare tankard variant which can only be found in the [[Mistlands]].
* If there is no mead in the player's inventory and they attempt to use the Tankard, a message will display, "You are out of mead" even though the model of the Tankard shows liquid inside.

The [[Building|construction system]] in ''Valheim'' implements a stability mechanic to encourage more realistic buildings and drive gameplay. If the player places a [[:Category:Building structures|building piece]] that is not sufficiently stable, it will collapse. Stability is primarily dictated by a piece's material, its position and orientation, and the pieces to which it is attached. Mechanically, the stability of a component is described by a number called its "''support''". This number is calculated and then checked to determine whether the component should break. A higher support value indicates more stability and less likelihood of breakage. The support system does not work like it does with real materials and resembles more how pressure propagates in a plumbing system. Or a magic force coming from ground and trees and flowing through the building pieces. For example, there is no limit on how many other pieces a single beam could support. == Materials == Each [[:Category:Building structures|building structure]] is made of one of several materials: {| class="wikitable" |+ Building Materials ! Name !! Prefixes !! MaxSupport !! MinSupport !! VerticalLoss !! HorizontalLoss |- | Wood || [[Wood Structures|Wood]], [[Thatch Roofs|Thatch roof]], [[Shingle Roofs|Shingle roof]], [[Darkwood Structures|Darkwood]], [[Ashwood Structures|Ashwood]] || {{Support|Wood|max}} || {{Support|Wood|min}} || {{Loss|Wood|vert}} || {{Loss|Wood|horiz}} |- | Hardwood || [[Log Structures|Log]] (core wood) || {{Support|Hard wood|max}} || {{Support|Hard wood|min}} || {{Loss|Hard wood|vert}} || {{Loss|Hard wood|horiz}} |- |Timberwood |[[Timber Structures|Timberwood]] |200 |10 |1/13 |1/5 |- | Stone || [[Stone Structures|Stone]] || {{Support|Stone|max}} || {{Support|Stone|min}} || {{Loss|Stone|vert}} || {{Loss|Stone|horiz}} |- | Iron || [[Wood Iron Structures|Wood iron]], [[Cage Structures|Cage]], [[Dvergr metal_wall|Dvergr metal]], [[Flametal Structures|Flametal]] || {{Support|Iron|max}} || {{Support|Iron|min}} || {{Loss|Iron|vert}} || {{Loss|Iron|horiz}} |- | Marble || [[Black Marble]] || {{Support|Marble|max}} || {{Support|Marble|min}} || {{Loss|Marble|vert}} || {{Loss|Marble|horiz}} |- | Ashstone || [[Grausten]] || {{Support|Ashstone|max}} || {{Support|Ashstone|min}} || {{Loss|Ashstone|vert}} || {{Loss|Ashstone|horiz}} |} The properties of the component's material influence its stability. * '''MaxSupport''': The maximum support value that a component can have. This is the support it will have if it is placed directly on the ground (or on natural features like rocks and trees). It will also be capped at this value if it is placed on something with a much higher support value (e.g. wood on well-supported stone). * '''MinSupport''': The minimum support value a component can have. If its support is less than or equal to this value, the item will break. * '''VerticalLoss / HorizontalLoss''': factors that influence how much support is lost for components that are built on other components rather than directly on the ground. == Support == A component is "''in contact''" with something when any part of its surface (including edges and corners) touches part of that other item's surface. When a component is directly in contact with the ground, its support is set to its material's MaxSupport value. When a component is not in contact with any other object, its support value will be zero and it will break. When a component is in contact only with other building components (called "''parents''"), its support will be calculated by a complex series of formula depending on the following factors: * Its material * The support values of each parent * The distances between it and each parent (distances are generally calculated from midpoints or centers of mass) * Its position relative to its parents === Single Parent === Before the support value can be calculated for a component that is supported by a single parent, two other values need to be calculated: ''distance'' and ''angled loss''. Both values depend on the relative locations of the two components' midpoints. The distance is calculated between centers of two pieces, using the standard [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pythagorean_theorem Pythagorean method]. However, a "fudge factor" of 0.1 meters is added to the distance for most calculations. Distance can generally be calculated with the following formula: Distance = SquareRoot( ([component's height]/2 + [parent's height]/2)2 + ([component's width]/2 + [parent's width]/2)2 ) + 0.1 For example, a Log pole 4m has a height of 4 meters and a width of 0, and a Log beam 2m has a width of 2 meters and a height of 0, so if a Log beam 2m is placed on a Log pole 4m (making a Г-shape), the distance between them will be 2.336 meters. The angled loss is calculated by interpolating between VerticalLoss and HorizontalLoss based on the angle between the component's midpoint and its parent's "''support point''". The parent's support point is usually (but not always) the point where the component is attached. Angled loss uses the following formula: Angle = cos-1( 1 - [height above support point] / [distance to support point] ) / π/2 NOTE: the "distance" in this formula does ''not'' include the 0.1 meter "fudge factor". In simple terms, this means: * when one piece is exactly above another, VerticalLoss value is used * when two pieces are connected horizontally, HorizontalLoss value is used * for all other situations the loss is somewhere between vertical and horizontal depending on how steep is the angle. E.g. in a strip of 45° roof, each next piece the coefficient would be (HorizontalLoss + VerticalLoss) / 2, for 26° it's 0.7 * HorizontalLoss + 0.3 * VerticalLoss
AngledLoss = [HorizontalLoss] * [Angle] + [VerticalLoss] * (1 - [Angle]) Once the distance and angled loss are obtained, the support can be calculated as follows: Support = [parent's support] * (1 - [AngledLoss] * [Distance]) For example, for the simple case of a Wood Pole 2m on top of another Wood Pole 2m that is on the ground, we can plug in the values as follows: Distance = 2.1 = SquareRoot( (2/2 + 2/2)2 + (0/2 + 0/2)2 ) + 0.1 Angle = 1 = cos-1( 1 - 1 / 1 ) / π/2 AngledLoss = 0.2 = 0.2 * 1 + 0.125 * (1 - 1) Support = 58 = 100 * (1 - 0.2 * 2.1) If we use 1-meter poles, the support will go as: Distance = 1.1 = SquareRoot( (1/2 + 1/2)2 + (0/2 + 0/2)2 ) + 0.1 Angle = 1 = cos-1( 1 - 1 / 1 ) / π/2 AngledLoss = 0.2 = 0.2 * 1 + 0.125 * (1 - 1) Support = 78 = 100 * (1 - 0.2 * 1.1) But obviously we go only 1 meter up this way, so if we need to calculate loss per 2 meters, we need to apply loss twice (square the number), which result in 60,84. Slightly more than using 2-meter poles, but the win is insignificant. === Multiple Parents === If a component is attached to multiple parents, the support from each individual parent is computed as in the single parent method, but total support is not just a sum of all parents. If two parents' support points are more than 100 degrees opposite each other (relative to the component) and are both below (at least 0.05 meters lower) the component's midpoint, the parents ''support'' the component ''together''. Any pair of parents can support a component together, even if one or both parents are already supporting the component with another parent. The support for a component is calculated similarly to single support, except that only VerticalLoss is used, regardless of the angle, and the two support values are averaged. Thus, the formula for Parent A and Parent B would be: MutualSupport = ( [Parent A's support] * (1 - [VerticalLoss] * [Distance to A]) + [Parent B's support] * (1 - [VerticalLoss] * [Distance to B]) ) / 2 Once all supports—single and double—have been calculated, the maximum support from all of them is chosen as the final support value for the component. A practical use of that feature is building non-ground stone floors. In a single support case, it is impossible to extend horizontally with stone, because HorizontalLoss for stone is 1 (i.e. 100% loss). But it is e.g. possible to build as big as 7x7 (49 blocks, 14x14 in meters) grid with stone floor pieces and metal support only on corners. Keep in mind that such structure holds together only as a whole, removing any block result in significant part of the structure falling apart. == Dynamic stability == Components do not break immediately, even if they are not properly supported. This is because support calculations are iterative, and must propagate throughout a structure before settling to their final values. When placed, a component's support is set to its Material's MaxSupport value. Then, every 0.5 seconds*, its support is calculated based on the current support values of its parents. This means, for example, that placing a component on another component but not touching anything else will often briefly raise the support value of its parent, because its parent views the component as a parent with a maxed support value. However, as the support value of the child component drops, it will cease to have an effect on the parent (because the parent is already better supported by other components). *A maximum of 50 components are recalculated every 0.5 seconds. Thus, in an area with many components, it may take longer. ---- '''Attribution''' All formulas and values were derived from the source code of Valheim, specifically the "''WearNTear.GetMaterialProperties''" and "''WearNTear.UpdateSupport''" functions. The '''Cartography Table''' was added in the [[Hearth & Home]] update. It is a table available in the build menu that allows the player to share their [[map]] and markers with another player.

One end of the table has a map, allowing players to add data to their own map, and the other end has a box to record their own discoveries onto the communal map. Map data discovered through the Cartography table can be distinguished from self-discovered data on the map and can be easily turned off.

== Map Markers ==
The last player that updates the table will have their markers on the map. This is so the table does not save every single marker players have placed.

* When the player has some copied pins on their map, they will appear dark-gray. Left-clicking them will turn them white and they will then be added to the player's markers.
* The player can toggle which type of markers they will see on the map. Right-click them on the right side of the map GUI and the player can toggle the groups on/off.<ref>[https://steamcommunity.com/app/892970/discussions/0/2950411088484630528/ Common issues in Hearth & Home]</ref>

'''Dvergr Tankards''' are an item used to consume [[Mead]] from within an inventory. Mead can, however, be consumed without the use of a tankard.

== Availability ==
Dvergr Tankards are found rarely inside [[Dvergr Guard Tower]]s and [[Dvergr Lighthouse]]s within the [[Mistlands]].  They appear as objects atop [[Dvergr (race)|Dvergr]] tables and can be picked up by interacting with them.

They can also be found rarely inside [[Infested Mine]]s, as loot inside treasure chests. Additionally, there are seven spawn locations for Dvergr Tankards in the lower floor of the [[Infested Citadel]] exterior; while still uncommon, the Dvergr Tankards have a higher chance of appearing at five of the seven Infested Citadel exterior spawns compared to at other Dvergr structures.

Due to a bug in the game in versions prior to [[Version history|version 0.213.4]], Dvergr Tankards in their "pickable"-object form (as opposed to their dropped-item form) will eventually fall and clip straight down through the structures they appear inside, coming to rest upon the terrain ''inside'' the floor of the structure; they ''can'' still be found there and picked up. Players looking for them in a Dvergr structure generated in versions prior to 0.213.4 should check inside the floors of the structure ''directly below'' any Dvergr tables it contains.

== Notes ==
* Despite its description, the Dvergr Tankard is functionally identical to the [[Tankard]] and the [[Horn of Celebration]].

'''Trinkets''' are [[items]] that can be equipped to provide various benefits during combat.

Equipping a trinket allows the player to gain [[Adrenaline]], which will be spent automatically to trigger the trinket's effect once enough adrenaline has been gained. Triggering twice the same trinket resets the effect timer.

Only one trinket can be equipped at a time. Removing a trinket does not cancel its activated effects, thus it is possible to accumulate multiple trinket effects by switching and activating each trinket.

All trinkets up until Mistlands-tier can be crafted at a Level 1 [[Forge]]. Mistlands-tier trinkets and onwards require Level 1 [[Black Forge]].

'''Archery Target''' is a structure used to train [[Bows (skill)]] and other ranged weapon skills.

Hitting the Archery Target only grants 35% of the normal [[Experience]] gain.

== Usage ==
When a projectile hits the target, it raises the skill of the weapon that fired it. The experience from a hit is highest in the center and falls off linearly with distance from it, reaching zero at the outer edge of the scoring area.

Each hit is given a score based on its distance from the center, which is shown on screen. Hovering over the target shows the most recent scores, the total score and the number of hits. A hit in the center plays a bullseye effect, with separate effects for two consecutive bullseyes and for a full row of bullseyes.

Interacting with the target resets its score and drops the recovered ammunition. The ammunition is also dropped if the target is destroyed.

== Building ==
The Archery Target is found in the Misc category of the [[Hammer]] and requires a nearby [[Workbench]] to build. It cannot be placed on floors or the ground; it must be attached to a wall or another vertical surface. It costs:
* {{Item link|Finewood|4}}
* {{Item link|Leather Scraps|10}}

It has 500 durability. It is immune to pierce, poison and spirit damage and weak to chop damage.

The Rustic Drawbridge can be built using:
* {{Item link|Silver|2}}
* {{Item link|Wolf Trophy|2}}
* {{Item link|Corewood|10}}

The Timberwood Drawbridge can be built using:
* {{Item link|Flametal|2}}
* {{Item link|Bloodgold|2}}
* {{Item link|Timberwood|24}}

==Usage==
A drawbridge works like a [[door]]. Interacting with it lowers it to form a bridge, and interacting again raises it back up to block the way. Like doors, drawbridges cannot be operated by players who lack access to a nearby [[Ward]].

Lowering the drawbridge deals 200 points of blunt (?) damage to any creature standing below, including the player character, which can easily kill them if not properly fed. This damage is reduced by armor and related resistances the creature might have. It is one of the types of death required to obtain the following achievement:

{{Achievement|DeathByAllTypes}}
